Graeme Lindsay Dwyer

Barefoot waterskiing's quiet world leader · master of stone · sportsman · father

From the lakes of Esperance to the rivers of the world, Graeme spent a lifetime at the water's edge — first as a barefoot skier, then as the administrator who led the sport worldwide. On land he was a craftsman in stone, restoring some of Sydney's great buildings. A life lived between motion and permanence.

A life in brief

One tide, running the length of a life

Graeme was born on 15 June 1937, his early years tied to Morawa in the Western Australian wheatbelt and then to Esperance on the southern coast, where football and open water shaped a natural sportsman.

He became a foundation figure of the West Australian Barefoot Club, a front-rank competitor through the 1970s, and — after moving east — a foundation member of the NSW Barefoot Club. Over three decades he gave the sport a lifetime of service, rising to chair its world council.

In Sydney he built a second craft entirely: Dwyer Heritage Restorations, a specialist stone and tuckpointing firm whose hands touched some of the city's landmark buildings. Later years were spent on the New South Wales South Coast and, finally, back home in Western Australia — with golf, the offshore boat Majestic, and family close by.

Barefoot waterskiing

He guarded the integrity of a world sport

Graeme's service ran from the club tow-rope to the top table of the world game. He managed Australia's World Championship team (1977–1980), served roughly ten years as Australian Technical Chairman, and was the official homologator — the person who certifies that the course, equipment and performances meet the rules — at the 1988 Melbourne and 1994 Sydney World Championships.

In August 1997, at Martigues in France, he was elected chairman of the IWSF World Barefoot Council unanimously, and re-elected unanimously in 2000. He carried barefooting's case onto the IWSF Executive Board, and on his watch the sport created its World Senior (Veterans) Championship at Penrith in 1998.

He was no armchair official. Before administration he was a competitor — third overall at the WA barefoot titles in both 1975 and 1976, club Technical Director by 1976, and an Australian veteran national champion in 1980.

One was helping guarantee the integrity of a world championship. The other was standing on its podium. — Graeme as homologator while his son Dodd took silver in jump, 1988 World Championships, Melbourne

The craftsman

A second craft, written in stone

In Sydney, Graeme built Dwyer Heritage Restorations — a specialist firm with more than thirty years in tuckpointing, repointing and sandstone restoration. The work was exacting and largely invisible when done well: the mark of a good restoration is that you cannot see it was ever needed.

The firm's hands reached some of the city's landmark buildings — a quiet civic legacy standing in stone across Sydney and beyond.

Beyond the water

Footballer, golfer, fisherman

Before the water there was football. A board kept by the family records Fairest & Best awards for Morawa (1957–59) and Newtown (1960–65), with further Esperance-association honours — as many as twelve awards across nine consecutive seasons.

Away from the tournament circuit there was golf with Gwen, and the water again — the family boat Majestic, moored on the Hacking River and run up into Sydney Harbour each summer for the New Year's Eve fireworks, and sometimes north past the Spit Bridge into the quiet of Bantry Bay.

Family

A father, first

For all the honours, Graeme's world was built around family — six children raised between Esperance and Sydney, and later years shared with Gwen on the South Coast and back home in the west.

His eldest, Dodd, followed him onto the water and became a world-record barefoot jumper. Father and son stood together at the 1988 World Championships — one certifying the contest, the other on its podium. Dodd sadly predeceased him.

This section is deliberately gentle and left for the family to shape — names, words and photographs are theirs to choose.
